title: MaxRL theory
text:
Maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) is a near-axiomatic principle: given data and a parametric family, choose parameters that maximize the probability (likelihood) of observed data. Given the ubiquity of MLE, it’s surprising that maximum-likelihood RL is this recent.

Classification is MLE: data-label pairs \((x, y) \sim \rho\), model \(p_\theta(y \mid x)\).
Regression is MLE: MSE corresponds to Gaussian noise MLE; L1 corresponds to Laplace noise MLE.
Diffusion (score-matching) is MLE, as shown in this post.

Why do we supervise with cross-entropy \(\mathbb E \log p_\theta(y\mid x)\) rather than accuracy-like \(\mathbb E\,p_\theta(y\mid x)\)? One mechanistic lens is the gradient: \[
\nabla_\theta \log p_\theta(y\mid x) = \frac{1}{p_\theta(y\mid x)}\,\nabla_\theta p_\theta(y\mid x).
\] So difficult cases (small \(p_\theta\)) get amplified by \(1/p_\theta\).

Maximum likelihood upweights difficult samples aggressively, updating the model on the frontier of its understanding.

Addendum: I would not over-interpret this as the principle itself. It’s a side-effect interpretation. The principle is still MLE. One canonical reading comes from information theory, where MLE is a compression objective that minimizes expected code length under the model. In this lens, each example contributes \(-\log p_\theta(y\mid x)\) nats of surprise. Hard examples are expensive in description length, so ML naturally prioritizes optimization there.

title: MaxRL theory
text:
Formulation, notation
Start in the standard LLM-RL latent-generation setting.

Data: \((x, y) \sim \rho\).
Policy/sequence model: \(z \sim m_\theta(\cdot \mid x)\), where \(z\) is a rollout.
Rollout evaluation: decode/postprocess \(z\) into a prediction; compare to target \(y\).

In binary reasoning with verifier, the typical objective is \[
J_{\mathrm{RL}} = \mathbb E_{(x,y)\sim\rho}\,\mathbb E_{z\sim m_\theta(\cdot\mid x)}\,\mathbf 1[\hat y(z)=y].
\]
So far this is standard RL setup. Now the useful abstraction.

A rollout \(z\) defines a predictive distribution \(\hat P(\cdot\mid z)\) over labels/targets.
Define per-rollout likelihood \[
l(y,z) := \hat P(y\mid z).
\]
Marginalize over rollouts: \[
\begin{equation}
p_\theta(y\mid x) := \mathbb E_{z\sim m_\theta(\cdot\mid x)} l(y,z).
\label{eq:marginal-likelihood}
\end{equation}
\]
Score function: \[
\begin{equation}
S(x,z) := \nabla_\theta \log m_\theta(z\mid x).
\label{eq:score}
\end{equation}
\]

This score vector is almost always the only intermediate through which policy parameters \(\theta\) touch policy-gradient objectives. Most algorithms differ mainly in how they reweight or shift these score vectors. Unpacking the latent-variable formulation already goes 60% of the way toward understanding this post; note that it subsumes supervised maximum likelihood when sampling is trivial.

title: MaxRL theory
section: Direct RL as a maximum-likelihood approximation
text:
Direct RL as a maximum-likelihood approximation
The maximum-likelihood objective (for our latent-generation likelihood) is \[
J(\theta)=\mathbb E_{(x,y)\sim\rho}\,\log p_\theta(y\mid x)
=\mathbb E_{(x,y)\sim\rho}\,\log\mathbb E_{z\sim m_\theta(\cdot\mid x)} l(y,z).
\] This is the exact analogue of cross-entropy: the log is outside the expectation because \(p_\theta(y\mid x)\) is a marginal likelihood.

Binary reasoning setup
In the binary reasoning setup, typical reward is the expected pass rate: \[
J_{\mathrm{pass}}
=
\mathbb E_{(x,y)\sim\rho}
\,\mathbb E_{z\sim m_\theta(\cdot\mid x)}\mathbf 1[\hat y(z)=y]
=
\mathbb E_{(x,y)\sim\rho}\,p_\theta(y\mid x).
\] Max-likelihood wants instead: \[
J_{\mathrm{ML}}
=
\mathbb E_{(x,y)\sim\rho}\,\log p_\theta(y\mid x)
=
\mathbb E_{(x,y)\sim\rho}\,\log\mathbb E_{z\sim m_\theta(\cdot\mid x)} \mathbf 1[\hat y(z)=y].
\]


Continuous regression
Specialize to a Gaussian noise model with \(\sigma=1\): \[
l(y,z)=\hat P(y\mid z)=\mathcal N(\hat y(z))(y)
=
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}
\exp\left[-\frac{(y-\hat y(z))^2}{2}\right].
\] Then \[
J(\theta)
=
\mathbb E_{(x,y)\sim\rho}
\,\log\mathbb E_{z\sim m_\theta(\cdot\mid x)}
\left[\exp\left(-\frac{(y-\hat y(z))^2}{2}\right)\right]
+\text{const}.
\]
An intuitive per-rollout reward is negative MSE: \[
r(y,z):=-\frac{(y-\hat y(z))^2}{2}.
\] A direct analogue would average these rollout rewards: \[
\mathbb E_{(x,y)\sim\rho}\,\mathbb E_{z\sim m_\theta(\cdot\mid x)}\,r(y,z).
\] Maximum likelihood instead optimizes \[
\mathbb E_{(x,y)\sim\rho}\,\log\mathbb E_{z\sim m_\theta(\cdot\mid x)}\,e^{r(y,z)}
\] this is (up to constants) a log-sum-exp, rather than a simple average, over per-rollout MSE-derived terms. So within each sample, the objective reinforces the most successful trajectories; we recover this same structure in the general form below.


Jenson and Taylor
Fix \((x,y)\) and suppress dependencies to reduce clutter: \[
p := p_\theta(y\mid x)=\mathbb E_{z\sim m_\theta(\cdot\mid x)} l(y,z).
\]
For \(p\in(0,1]\), Taylor-expanding about \(p=1\) yields \[
\log p
=
-\sum_{k=1}^\infty \frac{(1-p)^k}{k}.
\] The expansion is about \(p=1\) (success), so \(p\to 0\) implies greater deviation between the first (direct) and full (maximum-likelihood) degrees: another perspective on larger improvements for harder tasks.
Truncating to degree \(D\) gives the compute-indexed MaxRL objective \[
\begin{equation}
J_D(p)
:=
-\sum_{k=1}^D \frac{(1-p)^k}{k}.
\label{eq:j-truncated}
\end{equation}
\]

\(D=1\): \(J_1(p)=-(1-p)=p-1\), that is RL / pass-rate training up to an additive constant.
\(D\to\infty\): \(J_D(p)\to\log p\), that is exact maximum likelihood.

Differentiating: \[
\nabla_\theta J_D(p_\theta)
=
\sum_{k=1}^D (1-p)^{k-1} \cdot \nabla p
=: w_D(p)\cdot \nabla p
\] \[
\begin{equation}
w_D(p)=\sum_{k=0}^{D-1}(1-p)^k
=\frac{1-(1-p)^D}{p}.
\label{eq:weight}
\end{equation}
\] As \(D\to\infty\), \(w_D(p)\to 1/p\), recovering ML’s inverse-probability reweighting. The log-derivative trick on \(p=\mathbb E_{z\sim m_\theta}[l(y,z)]\) gives \[
\nabla_\theta p
= \mathbb E_{z\sim m_\theta(\cdot\mid x)}\big[l(y,z)\,\nabla_\theta\log m_\theta(z\mid x)\big]
=\mathbb E[lS],
\] so \[
\begin{equation}
\nabla_\theta J_D(p)
=
w_D(p)\,\mathbb E_{z\sim m_\theta(\cdot\mid x)}\big[l(y,z)\,S(x,z)\big].
\label{eq:gradient-main}
\end{equation}
\]
We can read off two qualitative behaviors:
Remark 1 (per-prompt): inside \(\mathbb E[lS]\), trajectories with larger likelihood \(l(y,z)\) get more weight.

Binary case: only successful rollouts contribute (\(l\in\{0,1\}\)).
Gaussian regression: \(l\propto \exp(-\mathrm{MSE}/(2\sigma^2))\) so the best rollouts dominate.

Remark 2 (across prompts): the scalar multiplier \(w_D(p)\) increases when \(p\) is small (hard prompts). In the ML limit \(D\to\infty\), \(w_D(p)=1/p\) reproduces the inverse-pass-rate reweighting.

title: MaxRL theory
text:
Gradient estimators
All’s great: we have a principled objective. How are we going about optimizing it?

Binary case
In the binary setting \(l(y,z)\in\{0,1\}\), draw \(N\) trajectories \(z_1,\dots,z_N\sim m_\theta(\cdot\mid x)\), define \[
l_j:=l(y,z_j),\qquad S_j:=\nabla_\theta\log m_\theta(z_j\mid x),\qquad K:=\sum_{j=1}^N l_j.
\]

REINFORCE (pass@1) uses \[
\hat g_{\mathrm{RL}}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^N l_j S_j,
\] which is unbiased for \(\nabla_\theta\,\mathrm{pass@}1(x)\).
MaxRL’s key estimator averages scores over successful trajectories only, \[
\begin{equation}
\hat g_N^{\mathrm{bin}}(x)
:=
\begin{cases}
\frac{1}{K}\sum_{j=1}^N l_j S_j, & K\ge 1,\\
0, & K=0.
\end{cases}
\label{eq:binary-estimator}
\end{equation}
\]

Conditioning on \(K\geq 1\), \[
\mathbb E_z\big[\hat g_N^{\mathrm{bin}}(x)\mid K\geq 1\big] = \mathbb E_z[S\mid l=1] = \dfrac{\mathbb E[l\cdot S]}{\mathbb E[l]} = \dfrac{\nabla p}{p} = \nabla \log p.
\] It’s an unbiased ML estimator, conditional on \(K\geq 1\)! The bias comes from \(K=0\), which occurs with probability \((1-p)^N\). Substituting recovers exactly the gradient form: \[
\mathbb E_z\big[\hat g_N^{\mathrm{bin}}(x)\big] = (1-(1-p)^N) \nabla \log p = w_N(p)\cdot \nabla p = \nabla J_N(p).
\]


Generalization
Drop the assumption \(l\in\{0,1\}\) and keep only what the derivation above actually used:

\(l_j := l(y,z_j)\in[0,1]\) is a per-rollout likelihood/reward signal,
\(p = \mathbb E[l]\),
\(\nabla_\theta p = \mathbb E[lS]\),
\(\nabla_\theta J_D = w_D(p)\,\nabla_\theta p\).

We want to estimate the last quantity using \(N\) iid rollout samples, with \(1 \le D \le N\). The obstacle is subtle but standard:

We can estimate \(p\) and \(\nabla_\theta p\) unbiasedly from samples.
But \(w_D(p)\nabla_\theta p\) is a product of unknowns.
Plugging in sample estimates makes bias because the factors are correlated.

The key is the leave-one-out trick. Use one sample to estimate \(\nabla_\theta p\), the remaining \(N-1\) samples to estimate \(w_D(p)\), and average over all leave-one-outs. The product factorizes because samples are conditionally independent.

We only need a known upper bound \(L \geq \max l\): set \(\sigma_j := l_j/L\), then \(\log\mathbb E[\sigma_j] = \log p - \log L\) differs by a \(\theta\)-independent constant, so the gradient is unchanged and all derivations apply with \((l_j, p) \mapsto (\sigma_j, \sigma_\theta)\). For Gaussian regression, \(L = (2\pi\sigma^2)^{-1/2}\).

Formally, suppose we have an estimator subroutine \(\omega_j\), built from \(\{l_k\}_{k\ne j}\) only, such that \[
\mathbb E[\omega_j] = w_D(p).
\] We know \(l_j S_j\) is an unbiased estimator for \(\nabla p = \mathbb E[l\cdot S]\), so the leave-one-out product \(\omega_j l_j \cdot S_j\) is unbiased for \(w_D(p)\nabla_\theta p\). Averaging over \(j\) gives the final estimator: \[
\begin{equation}
\hat g_D(x,y)
:=
\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^N \omega_j\,l_j\,S_j.
\label{eq:general-estimator}
\end{equation}
\] This is, again, a simple reweighted average of the rollout scores. To reduce variance, we can subtract any constant baseline (since \(\mathbb E[S]=0\)).
It remains to solve: given iid samples \((l_0, \dots, l_{N-1})\), estimate \(w_D(p)=\sum_{k=0}^{D-1}(1-p)^k\).

Taking \(D=N\), it suffices to obtain estimators for \((1-p)^k\) for all \(1\leq k\leq N-1\).
This is a textbook problem with a known MVUE (minimum-variance unbiased estimator). See Gradient Estimator for the numerically stable \(O(BRD)\) prefix-suffix-scan implementation used in this repo.



Generalized baseline subtraction
Here, we explain the semantics of MaxRLEstimatorConfig.subtract_baseline flag.
The leave-one-out construction admits more than a constant baseline. Since \(\omega_j\) is built from the peers \(z_{-j} := (z_i)_{i \ne j}\) only, any \(b_j\) measurable with respect to \(z_{-j}\) preserves unbiasedness, and replacing the per-rollout coefficient \(c_j := \omega_j l_j\) by \(c_j - b_j\) leaves an unbiased estimator of \(\nabla_\theta J_D(p)\). Consider the peer-only baseline \[
b_j := \omega_j\,\bar l_{-j}, \qquad \bar l_{-j} := \frac{1}{N-1}\sum_{i\ne j} l_i,
\] and the centered coefficient becomes \[
a_j := c_j - b_j = \omega_j\,(l_j - \bar l_{-j}) = \omega_j \cdot \frac{N}{N-1}\,(l_j - \bar l),
\] with \(\bar l := \frac{1}{N}\sum_i l_i\), via the identity \(l_j - \bar l_{-j} = \frac{N}{N-1}(l_j - \bar l)\). The baseline-subtracted estimator \[
\hat g_D^{\mathrm c}(x, y) := \frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^N a_j\,S_j
\] is unbiased for \(\nabla_\theta J_D(p)\), and strip the common \(\omega_j p\) level shared across rollouts.

A tempting alterantive is the leave-one-out average of \((\omega l)_{-j}\), but this quantity is measurable w.r.t. \(z_j\) because \(\omega_{k\neq j}\) is dependent upon \(z_j\), resulting in a biased estimator.

title: MaxRL Statistics
text:
Continuously updated research progress on the rollout-likelihood generalization of maximum likelihood reinforcement learning.
Theory:

Theory — MaxRL as a compute-indexed truncation of log-likelihood, per-rollout reweighting, and the generalized leave-one-out estimator.
Gradient Estimator — numerically stable \(O(BRD)\) computation of the leave-one-out weights via prefix-suffix scans of elementary symmetric polynomials.

Experiments:

Regression: bag of words — noise-robustness in the zero-step sampling setting.
Regression: corpus regression — same zero-step setting on natural-language prefixes. WIP.
Scalar pretrain — scalar-observation LM pretraining with hidden token states. WIP.
Code Regression — CDSS memory prediction with RegressLM CE pretraining, SL-MSE, RLOO, and MaxRL. WIP.

title: Code Regression
text: The code-regression setup asks whether we can predict execution-memory statistics from source code. Our current slice takes the CDSS rows from the Code-Regression dataset and predicts the memory target from the submitted program text. The broader dataset and RegressLM baseline are described in Regression Language Models for Code; our current model family uses T5Gemma encoders and compares supervised regression with rollout-based MaxRL methods from Maximum Likelihood Reinforcement Learning.

title: Code Regression
text:
Problem setup
Each row is a code submission with metadata and a scalar memory target. After preprocessing, we keep only CDSS examples and format the model input as
# CDSS
# Language: Python
<source code>
where Python is replaced by the metadata language when available. The prediction target has two current forms:

Raw memory. target = memory_bytes, copied from the original dataset target column after filtering finite CDSS rows.
Per-language quantile-normalized memory. Within each CDSS language, raw memory values are ranked and mapped through the standard normal inverse CDF. This keeps ordering inside each language while removing language-specific scale and marginal-shape differences.

Let \(X\) denote the formatted code prompt, \(Y_{\mathrm{raw}}\) the raw memory value, and \(Y_{\mathrm{qn}}\) the quantile-normalized value. In either variant the supervised target is a scalar \[
Y \in \mathbb{R},
\] and the ideal predictor is the conditional mean \[
g^\ast(x) := \mathbb{E}[Y \mid X=x].
\] The main held-out risk is therefore \[
\mathcal{E}(\theta)
  :=
  \mathbb{E}\left[(g_\theta(X)-Y)^2\right].
\]
The raw target is the literal memory-prediction task. The quantile-normalized target turns the question toward within-language ranking and calibration: can the model place a submission correctly relative to other submissions in the same programming language? Performance on this normalized target should be read as evidence about relative memory behavior inside each language. Raw-byte performance additionally tests whether the model can handle the cross-language unit scale.
Output-side tokenization adds one more layer of notation. Let \[
\mathcal{Z}
\] be the finite set of syntactically valid decoder token sequences under the P10 grammar, and let \[
\phi:\mathcal{Z}\to\mathbb{R}
\] be the deterministic parser that extracts the numeric value represented by a complete token sequence. A language-model decoder defines a conditional distribution \[
q_\theta(z\mid x),\qquad z\in\mathcal{Z}.
\] The latent rollout is the token sequence \(Z\sim q_\theta(\cdot\mid x)\); the decoded prediction candidate is the scalar \(\phi(Z)\).
The targeted regression problem follows the scalar label \(Y\). Token strings enter as one way to produce candidate numeric values. For example, if the final predictor is the median of decoded samples, then the induced predictor is \[
m_\theta(x) := \operatorname{median}\{\phi(Z):Z\sim q_\theta(\cdot\mid x)\},
\] and the corresponding scalar risk is \[
\mathbb{E}\left[(m_\theta(X)-Y)^2\right].
\] Training methods below use different surrogates for this target. Many token sequences can parse to the same number: \[
\mathcal{Z}(v) := \{z\in\mathcal{Z}: \phi(z)=v\}
\] can contain several valid strings.

title: Code Regression
text:
Methods
The current methods combine two related architectures with three objective families. CE pretraining and LM-RL both use an encoder-decoder language model over numeric target tokens. CE learns the canonical token string itself. LM-RLOO and LM-MaxRL sample token strings, parse them to numbers, and optimize scalar reward or likelihood of the parsed value. The regression-head route keeps the T5Gemma encoder idea and predicts through a direct scalar value head, trained with SL-MSE, RLOO, or MaxRL.

CE pretraining - text-to-number language modeling
pretrain_code_regression trains a RegressLM-style conditional decoder. The encoder reads the code prompt, and the decoder autoregressively emits a fixed P10 scientific-notation representation of the scalar target. With the default P10 tokenizer, one number uses
\[
2 + d = 6
\]
tokens: one sign token, four mantissa digit tokens, and one exponent token. For example, under the default four-digit P10 representation,
256.0   -> <+> <2> <5> <6> <0> <E-1>
-1.25   -> <-> <1> <2> <5> <0> <E-3>
0.1234  -> <+> <1> <2> <3> <4> <E-4>
The table below shows representative raw and quantile-normalized CDSS targets under this P10 tokenization.

  

The important detail is that training is ordinary language modeling. If \(c(Y) = (Z^c_1,\dots,Z^c_L)\) is the canonical target tokenization of the numeric label, the model minimizes token-level cross entropy \[
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}}(\theta)
  =
  -\mathbb{E}
  \left[
    \frac{1}{L}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}
      \log q_\theta(Z^c_\ell \mid X, Z^c_{<\ell})
  \right].
\]






NoteCE learns a numeric spelling



CE pretraining learns a symbolic sign-digit-exponent sequence. Numeric scale enters through the tokenizer’s rounding, clipping, and exponent range, so a single token error can have very different scalar consequences depending on whether it lands in the mantissa or exponent. The digit targets are discrete classes: predicting <6> means assigning probability to the token class <6>. This makes CE a useful RegressLM-style baseline and also makes token likelihood an indirect proxy for numeric MSE.


There is an additional representation issue. The P10 grammar allows valid non-canonical strings with leading zero mantissas, and multiple valid strings can decode to exactly the same number. For example,
<+> <1> <0> <0> <0> <E-3>  -> 1.0
<+> <0> <1> <0> <0> <E-2>  -> 1.0
<+> <0> <0> <1> <0> <E-1>  -> 1.0
<+> <0> <0> <0> <1> <E0>   -> 1.0
CE assigns training mass to the single string selected by the canonicalizer \(c(y)\). Numerically equivalent strings receive no target mass under this CE objective, even though \(\phi(z)\) is correct. When the exact label falls outside the finite P10 grid or between grid points, the canonicalizer first rounds or clips to a representable token string. Thus the CE population target is \[
q^\ast_{\mathrm{CE}}(z\mid x)
  =
  \mathbb{P}(c(Y)=z\mid X=x),
\] The corresponding set-valued numeric target is \[
\mathcal{Z}(Y)=\{z:\phi(z)=Y\}.
\] For deterministic labels and infinite model capacity this distinction can be small, because the canonical string decodes to a good numeric approximation. For finite models it matters: probability mass on a numerically equivalent non-canonical rollout helps scalar prediction while receiving no CE credit.
Decoding is also language-model-like. At each decoder step, impossible P10 tokens are masked out: the first position can only be a sign, middle positions are digits, and the final position is an exponent token. Evaluation samples 64 complete numeric decodes per example and reports the median decoded value before computing scalar metrics.


LM-RL - token rollouts with scalar rewards
LM-RL keeps the same constrained language-model policy as CE and changes the object being optimized. We draw rollout token sequences from the model itself: \[
Z_j \sim q_{\theta,T}(\cdot\mid x),\qquad j=1,\dots,R,
\] where \(T>0\) is the sampling temperature used for both sampling and sequence log-probabilities. Each rollout is parsed to a scalar \[
V_j := \phi(Z_j).
\] The loss functions then compare \(V_j\) to the exact target value \(y\) stored in the dataset. The learning signal rewards token strings whose extracted number is close to \(y\).
The sequence score used by policy gradients is \[
\log q_{\theta,T}(Z_j\mid x)
  =
  \sum_{\ell=1}^L
  \log q_{\theta,T}(Z_{j,\ell}\mid x,Z_{j,<\ell}),
\] with the same P10 validity mask as CE decoding. The sampled scalar values are detached when constructing rewards or score weights; gradients flow through the sequence log-probability.

LM-RLOO
LM-RLOO uses negative squared scalar error as the reward: \[
r_j := -(V_j-y)^2.
\] For \(R\geq 2\) rollouts, the leave-one-out advantage is \[
A_j
  =
  r_j - \frac{1}{R-1}\sum_{k\ne j} r_k
  =
  \frac{R}{R-1}(r_j-\bar r),
\qquad
\bar r := \frac{1}{R}\sum_{k=1}^R r_k.
\] The minibatch surrogate minimized in code is \[
\widehat{\mathcal{L}}_{\mathrm{LM\mbox{-}RLOO}}
  =
  -\frac{1}{BR}
  \sum_{b=1}^B\sum_{j=1}^R
    A_{b,j}\log q_{\theta,T}(Z_{b,j}\mid x_b),
\] where \(A_{b,j}\) is detached. The corresponding population objective is \[
J_{\mathrm{LM\mbox{-}RLOO}}(\theta)
  =
  \mathbb{E}_{X,Y}
  \mathbb{E}_{Z\sim q_{\theta,T}(\cdot\mid X)}
  \left[-(\phi(Z)-Y)^2\right].
\] Equivalently, LM-RLOO minimizes the expected squared error of decoded token rollouts: \[
\mathbb{E}_{X,Y,Z}\left[(\phi(Z)-Y)^2\right].
\] Thus all token strings with the same decoded value are interchangeable to LM-RLOO. If \(\phi(z)=y\) exactly, the reward is zero regardless of whether \(z\) is the canonical P10 string.


LM-MaxRL
LM-MaxRL replaces the raw squared-error reward by a normalized Gaussian likelihood score. Let \(\tau>0\) denote score_std. For a rollout \(z\), define \[
s_\tau(y,z)
  :=
  \exp\left(-\frac{(\phi(z)-y)^2}{2\tau^2}\right)
  \in (0,1].
\] This is the Gaussian observation likelihood \(\mathcal{N}(y;\phi(z),\tau^2)\) divided by its supremum \((\sqrt{2\pi}\tau)^{-1}\), so the maximum possible score is one. For one example, the marginal normalized likelihood under the LM policy is \[
S_{\theta,\tau}(x,y)
  :=
  \mathbb{E}_{Z\sim q_{\theta,T}(\cdot\mid x)}
  [s_\tau(y,Z)].
\]
The degree-\(D\) MaxRL target is the truncated log-likelihood objective \[
J_D(\theta)
  =
  \mathbb{E}_{X,Y}
  \left[
    -\sum_{k=1}^{D}
    \frac{(1-S_{\theta,\tau}(X,Y))^k}{k}
  \right].
\] As \(D\to\infty\) this becomes \[
J_\infty(\theta)
  =
  \mathbb{E}_{X,Y}\left[\log S_{\theta,\tau}(X,Y)\right].
\]
The sampled implementation uses the same leave-one-out MaxRL estimator described in MaxRL gradient estimator details. For sampled scores \(s_j=s_\tau(y,Z_j)\), define complements \(a_j=1-s_j\). The leave-one-out weight for rollout \(j\) is \[
\omega_j
  =
  \sum_{k=0}^{D-1}
  \frac{e_k((a_i)_{i\ne j})}{\binom{R-1}{k}},
\] where \(e_k\) is the \(k\)-th elementary symmetric polynomial and \(e_0=1\). The current LM-MaxRL recipe always subtracts a rollout baseline: \[
s^{\mathrm{eff}}_j
  =
  \frac{R}{R-1}(s_j-\bar s),
\qquad
\bar s := \frac{1}{R}\sum_{i=1}^{R}s_i.
\] The surrogate loss is \[
\widehat{\mathcal{L}}_{\mathrm{LM\mbox{-}MaxRL}}
  =
  -\frac{1}{BR}
  \sum_{b=1}^{B}\sum_{j=1}^{R}
    \omega_{b,j}s^{\mathrm{eff}}_{b,j}
    \log q_{\theta,T}(Z_{b,j}\mid x_b),
\] with the weights detached. By default, the implementation uses \(D=R\) unless a separate degree is provided.


Optimization targets and limits
The CE and LM-RL methods can share a decoder and tokenizer while optimizing different population quantities:








Method
Population target
What is treated as correct?




CE pretraining
Maximize \(\mathbb{E}[\log q_\theta(c(Y)\mid X)]\) token by token
Only the canonical token string \(c(Y)\)


LM-RLOO
Maximize \(\mathbb{E}[-(\phi(Z)-Y)^2]\) for \(Z\sim q_{\theta,T}(\cdot\mid X)\)
Any rollout whose decoded number is close to \(Y\)


LM-MaxRL
Maximize \(J_D\) or, as \(D\to\infty\), \(\mathbb{E}[\log \mathbb{E}_{Z\sim q_{\theta,T}(\cdot\mid X)}s_\tau(Y,Z)]\)
Any rollout with high Gaussian score after decoding









NoteShared decoder, different target



CE, LM-RLOO, and LM-MaxRL can use the same P10 decoder while learning from different signals. CE concentrates probability on a canonical string. LM-RLOO and LM-MaxRL score decoded scalar values, so token strings that parse to the same useful number are equivalent for the rollout objective.


CE has no training rollout count or score standard deviation. As the evaluation sample count grows, its reported median prediction converges to the median of \(\phi(Z)\) under the learned decoder distribution. This affects evaluation Monte Carlo error while leaving the CE training target unchanged.
As the number of LM-RL training rollouts \(R\) grows, LM-RLOO converges to the exact policy gradient of \(J_{\mathrm{LM\mbox{-}RLOO}}\). The leave-one-out baseline leaves the population target unchanged and changes estimator variance. LM-MaxRL converges to the gradient of the degree-\(D\) MaxRL target when \(D\) is fixed. Under the default choice \(D=R\), sending \(R\to\infty\) also sends \(D\to\infty\), so the target approaches the log marginal score \(J_\infty\).
The score_std limit only applies directly to LM-MaxRL and is separate from the rollout sampling temperature. LM-RLOO has no score_std hyperparameter in the current implementation. For LM-MaxRL:

As \(\tau\to 0\), \(s_\tau(y,z)\) approaches an indicator of exact numeric equality \(\phi(z)=y\). If \(y\) is exactly representable, the limiting objective rewards the total probability of all exact representations \(\sum_{z:\phi(z)=y}q_\theta(z\mid x)\), including non-canonical strings. If \(y\) falls between representable decoded values, the signal concentrates on the nearest grid points and can become extremely sparse in finite rollouts.
As \(\tau\to\infty\), \(s_\tau(y,z)=1-(\phi(z)-y)^2/(2\tau^2)+O(\tau^{-4})\). Therefore \(\log S_{\theta,\tau}(x,y)\) is \(-\mathbb{E}_{Z}[(\phi(Z)-y)^2]/(2\tau^2)+O(\tau^{-4})\) up to constants. The target becomes expected decoded MSE, and the gradient scale vanishes like \(\tau^{-2}\).

For LM-RLOO, introducing an artificial reward scale \(-(\phi(z)-y)^2/(2\tau^2)\) would leave the optimum unchanged for any finite \(\tau>0\) and would simply rescale the gradient. The current code fixes this scale implicitly by using \(-(\phi(z)-y)^2\).



Regression-head model
The regression-head methods use a deterministic scalar predictor \[
g_\theta(x) \in \mathbb{R}.
\] The architecture is a T5Gemma encoder, a learned one-token query passed through a transformer decoder over the encoder memory, and a linear value head. In code, the model predicts from the decoded query state: \[
g_\theta(x)
  =
  w^\top h_\theta(x) + b.
\]
This architecture removes the numeric tokenizer from the output side. The model is judged directly in the same scalar space as the target variant being trained: raw bytes for the raw task, or normal scores for the quantile-normalized task.


SL-MSE - direct scalar regression
The supervised regression baseline minimizes the same squared error used by the primary evaluation: \[
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SL\mbox{-}MSE}}(\theta)
  =
  \mathbb{E}\left[(g_\theta(X)-Y)^2\right].
\]
For a minibatch, \[
\widehat{\mathcal{L}}_{\mathrm{SL\mbox{-}MSE}}
  =
  \frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}
    (g_\theta(x_b)-y_b)^2.
\]
This is the cleanest reference objective: if the evaluation target is MSE, then SL-MSE optimizes it directly. It uses no rollouts, likelihood temperatures, tokenization choices, or policy-gradient estimator.


RLOO - Gaussian rollout policy with leave-one-out rewards
RLOO turns the scalar predictor into the mean of a Gaussian rollout policy: \[
Z_j \sim \pi_\theta(\cdot \mid x)
      =
      \mathcal{N}(g_\theta(x), \sigma^2),
\qquad j=1,\dots,R.
\]
The reward is negative squared error against the scalar target: \[
r_j = -(Z_j - y)^2.
\]
The leave-one-out advantage is \[
A_j
  =
  r_j - \frac{1}{R-1}\sum_{k\ne j}r_k
  =
  \frac{R}{R-1}(r_j-\bar r),
\qquad
\bar r := \frac{1}{R}\sum_{k=1}^{R}r_k.
\]
The score-function surrogate is \[
\widehat{\mathcal{L}}_{\mathrm{RLOO}}
  =
  -\frac{1}{BR}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\sum_{j=1}^{R}
    A_{b,j}\,
    \log \pi_\theta(Z_{b,j}\mid x_b),
\] with the sampled advantages detached.
The leave-one-out baseline is unbiased because it depends only on peer rollouts for the current example. In the population limit, \[
\mathbb{E}_{Z\sim\mathcal{N}(g_\theta(x),\sigma^2)}
  [-(Z-y)^2]
  =
  -(g_\theta(x)-y)^2 - \sigma^2.
\] The extra \(\sigma^2\) term is independent of \(\theta\), so maximizing expected RLOO reward has the same optimum and gradient direction as minimizing scalar MSE. Finite \(R\) changes the variance of the gradient estimator while preserving the population target.


MaxRL - likelihood-weighted rollout estimator
MaxRL uses the same Gaussian rollout policy, \[
Z_j \sim \mathcal{N}(g_\theta(x),\sigma^2),
\] and scores each rollout by a Gaussian observation likelihood of the target: \[
\ell_y(z)
  =
  \mathcal{N}(y; z, \sigma^2).
\]
The supremum of this one-dimensional likelihood is \[
L = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma},
\] so the normalized likelihood is \[
\sigma_j
  :=
  \frac{\ell_y(Z_j)}{L}
  =
  \exp\left(-\frac{(Z_j-y)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)
  \in (0,1].
\]
For one example, define the marginal normalized likelihood \[
\sigma_\theta(x,y)
  :=
  \mathbb{E}_{Z\sim\pi_\theta(\cdot\mid x)}
    [\sigma_y(Z)].
\] The degree-\(M\) MaxRL objective is the same truncation used in MaxRL gradient estimator details: \[
J_M(\theta)
  =
  -\sum_{k=1}^{M}
    \frac{(1-\sigma_\theta)^k}{k}.
\] As \(M\to\infty\), this approaches \[
J_\infty(\theta) = \log \sigma_\theta.
\]
The sampled estimator forms leave-one-out weights from the peer complements \(a_i = 1-\sigma_i\). For rollout \(j\), \[
\omega_j
  =
  \sum_{k=0}^{M-1}
  \frac{
    e_k((a_i)_{i\ne j})
  }{
    \binom{R-1}{k}
  },
\] where \(e_k\) is the \(k\)-th elementary symmetric polynomial. With baseline subtraction, the effective normalized likelihood term is \[
\sigma^{\mathrm{eff}}_j
  =
  \frac{R}{R-1}(\sigma_j-\bar\sigma),
\qquad
\bar\sigma := \frac{1}{R}\sum_{i=1}^{R}\sigma_i.
\] The policy-gradient surrogate is \[
\widehat{\mathcal{L}}_{\mathrm{MaxRL}}
  =
  -\frac{1}{BR}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\sum_{j=1}^{R}
    \omega_{b,j}\sigma^{\mathrm{eff}}_{b,j}
    \log \pi_\theta(Z_{b,j}\mid x_b),
\] with the score weights detached.
In the exact Gaussian limit, MaxRL also reduces to MSE. The convolution identity gives \[
\mathbb{E}_{Z\sim\mathcal{N}(g_\theta(x),\sigma^2)}
  [\mathcal{N}(y;Z,\sigma^2)]
  =
  \mathcal{N}(y;g_\theta(x),2\sigma^2),
\] so \[
\log \sigma_\theta(x,y)
  =
  -\frac{(g_\theta(x)-y)^2}{4\sigma^2}
  + \mathrm{const}.
\] Thus the infinite-rollout MaxRL objective is a positive rescaling of negative MSE plus a constant. As with RLOO, the finite-rollout estimator is the interesting object: it changes how noisy or selective the update is while the ideal scalar target remains MSE in this Gaussian setup.

title: Code Regression
text:
Evaluation
This writeup focuses on CDSS metrics. The primary keys are







Metric key
Meaning




eval-core/mse/space/CDSS
pooled CDSS mean squared error


eval-core/mae/space/CDSS
pooled CDSS mean absolute error


eval-core/spearman/space/CDSS
pooled CDSS Spearman rank correlation




  


Evaluation set construction
The eval set is balanced by CDSS language. For each cdss_language/<language> group, the cache builder keeps at most eval_cap_per_group examples; in the current Modal recipes this cap is 256. Languages with at least 256 valid CDSS examples enter the evaluation. Thus, if \(|\mathcal{L}|\) languages survive the threshold, the pooled CDSS eval set contains exactly \[
256 \cdot |\mathcal{L}|
\] examples, with the same number of examples from each retained language.
Selection is deterministic: examples are ordered by a stable hash of their identifier, then capped within language. Each retained row is assigned both its auxiliary language group, such as cdss_language/Python, and the pooled space/CDSS group.
The pooled CDSS metric treats all selected CDSS eval examples as one population. For MSE, with selected CDSS pairs \((y_i,\hat y_i)\), \[
\widehat{\mathrm{MSE}}_{\mathrm{CDSS}}
  =
  \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}(\hat y_i-y_i)^2.
\] MAE is the same pooled average with absolute error, and Spearman is computed once over the pooled CDSS target and prediction vectors.
Language-mean metrics shift the estimand. The auxiliary cdss_language/<language> groups first compute a metric within each language. Then eval-core/<metric>/space/CDSS_language_mean averages those language scores equally: \[
\widehat{m}_{\mathrm{language\ mean}}
  =
  \frac{1}{|\mathcal{L}|}
  \sum_{\ell\in\mathcal{L}}
    \widehat{m}_\ell.
\]
The decoder-LM and regression-head routes produce predictions differently before metrics are computed:

CE pretraining, LM-RLOO, and LM-MaxRL sample numeric decodes and use the per-example median decoded value as the prediction.
Regression-head methods produce one deterministic scalar prediction \(g_\theta(x)\).

After that, all methods are evaluated with the same target/prediction metric code.

title: Code Regression
text:
Critical notes

Raw memory and quantile-normalized memory are different tasks. Raw memory tests physical scale prediction; the normalized target tests within-language relative memory prediction.
CE pretraining is a strong RegressLM-style baseline, but its loss is token CE over one canonical P10 string, not numeric MSE. A CE improvement can come from better exponent/sign/digit likelihood without matching scalar error improvements one-for-one.
LM-RL fixes the specific CE mismatch caused by non-unique tokenization: it scores the decoded number \(\phi(z)\), so numerically equivalent strings are equivalent to the objective. It does not remove finite-rollout variance or finite-grid representability issues.
In the current one-dimensional Gaussian rollout setup, RLOO and MaxRL have MSE as their exact infinite-rollout target up to constants or scale. Any empirical gap against SL-MSE should be interpreted as finite-rollout estimator behavior, optimizer interaction, or architecture/training difference, not as a fundamentally different Bayes target.

title: Regression: bag of words
text: The bag-of-words (BoW) setup isolates noise-robustness of SL, GRPO, and MaxRL in a zero-step rollout setting: the model sees a single prompt and predicts a scalar target with no sequential reasoning. There are three versions of the dataset:

title: Regression: bag of words
text:
Dataset

Homogeneous baseline
See src/data/bag_of_words.py.
Each prompt is \(L\) words sampled iid from a mixture of semantic words, which carries signal, and auxiliary words, which are pure fillers. The target is a noise-corrupted linear function of word content, parameterized by the correlation between signal and target \(\rho \in (0, 1]\).
7-word vocabulary. Semantic words map to integer values centered at zero:



grim
bad
poor
fair
good
great
perfect




\(-3\)
\(-2\)
\(-1\)
\(0\)
\(+1\)
\(+2\)
\(+3\)



The 256 auxiliary words (common function words: the, a, and, if, because, …) carry value 0. We also define variants with more (e.g. \(11\), \(15\)) semantic words.
Sampling distribution. Semantic words share mass \(1 - \alpha\) (where \(\alpha\) = aux_words_ratio), shaped by a power-law centered on the neutral word “fair”: \(p_i \propto (1 + |i - \text{center}|)^{-\gamma}\). Auxiliary words uniformly split mass \(\alpha\).



Semantic word probabilities at canonical configuration when half of the words are semantic, with linearly decaying frequency: \(\alpha = 0.5, \gamma = 1.0\)


Target generation. Given a prompt of length \(L\): \[
\text{signal} = \frac{\rho}{\sigma\sqrt{L}} \sum_{i=1}^L v_i, \qquad
\text{target} = \text{signal} + \mathcal{N}(0, \sqrt{1 - \rho^2})
\] where \(\sigma\) is the per-token standard deviation under the full mixture (zero mean by symmetry). By construction \(\text{Var}(\text{target}) = 1\) and \(\text{corr}(\text{signal}, \text{target}) = \rho\).






NoteExamples





Consider 8-word prompts; we compute the per-word signal stdev \(\sigma = 1.14\), so the per-prompt stdev \(\sqrt{L}\,\sigma = 3.21\). Semantic words are bolded:
Low-signal regime: \(\rho = 0.01\) — multiplier \(\rho / (\sigma \sqrt{L}) = 0.0031\), noise stdev \(\sqrt{1 - \rho^2} \approx 1.00\):

both idea fair poor rather bad grim then

\(\sum v_i = -6\), signal \(= 0.0031 \times (-6) = -0.019\), target \(= -2.54\)
High-signal regime: \(\rho = 0.89\) — multiplier \(= 0.277\), noise stdev \(\sqrt{1 - \rho^2} = 0.46\):

good good floor good good good perfect poor

\(\sum v_i = +7\), signal \(= 0.277 \times 7 = 1.94\), target \(= 1.78\)









Word-level heteroskedasticity (learnable)
We propose another heteroskedastic variation where hardness is tied to word content, so it is in principle recoverable from the prompt. Semantic words are ranked by \(|v(w)|\) and assigned a quantile \(q(w) \in (0, 1)\); auxiliary words carry zero hardness. The dataset is parameterized by global signal-to-target correlation \(\rho\), and a difficulty skew snr_halflife_in_word_quantile






NoteConstruction details





The raw per-word multiplier is \[
\tilde a(w) \;=\; \begin{cases} 2^{(q(w) - 1/2)\,/\,h_{\text{word}}} & w \text{ semantic},\\ 0 & w \text{ auxiliary}, \end{cases}
\] with \(h_{\text{word}}\) = snr_halflife_in_word_quantile. For a prompt \(x = (w_1, \dots, w_L)\) the prompt-level multiplier is the per-token RMS \[
\tilde a(x)^2 = \frac{1}{L} \sum_{j=1}^{L} \tilde a(w_j)^2,
\qquad
a(x) = \tilde a(x) \,/\, \sqrt{\mathbb{E}_{w \sim p}[\tilde a(w)^2]},
\] so that \(\mathbb{E}[a(x)^2] = 1\) under the prompt distribution. Targets still preserve the global correlation \(\rho\): \[
\text{target}(x) = \text{signal}(x) + \sqrt{1-\rho^2}\, a(x)\, \varepsilon,
\]

title: Regression: corpus regression
text: The corpus-regression task performs next-token regression on natural-language prefixes streamed from HuggingFaceFW/fineweb-edu. Difficulty now comes from real text rather than a hand-tuned signal-to-noise schedule.

title: Regression: corpus regression
text:
Problem setup
Fix a document distribution \(p\) over fineweb-edu and a prefix length \(n = L = 128\). Pick a deterministic observation function \(f : V \to \mathbb{R}^k\) on the tokenizer vocabulary \(V\). The task is to predict the conditional expectation of \(f\) at the \(K\)-th lookahead token from the prefix only: \[
g(x_{1:n}) \;:=\; \mathbb{E}_{x_{n+K} \,\sim\, p(\cdot \mid x_{1:n})}\, f(x_{n+K}),
\] using a parametric estimator \(g_\theta\). Intermediate tokens \(x_{n+1}, \dots, x_{n+K-1}\) are not exposed to the model; with \(K = 1\) this collapses to next-token expectation, and with \(K > 1\) it is a skip-ahead target. The same fineweb-edu sample is therefore truncated to its first \(n + K\) tokens, the prefix is the first \(n\), and the label is derived from the token at position \(n + K\) alone.
Two label families are implemented in src/data/corpus_regression.py (lines 81–202):

token_id (current canonical setting). \(k = 1\). Either the raw integer id \(f(t) = t\), or, when normalize_labels=True, the rescaled \(f(t) = \mathrm{lo} + (\mathrm{hi} - \mathrm{lo})\cdot t / |V|\) on the configured label_range (canonical (0.0, 1.0)). The _enforce_token_id_dim validator forces embedding_dim = 1 whenever this label type is selected, so all formulas below carry through with \(D = 1\) for the current sweeps.
rademacher (earlier variant, kept in code). \(k = D = 32\). \(f(t)\) is the row of a vocab-keyed \(\pm 1\) matrix _rademacher_matrix (manual_seed(0), lines 157–164) — deterministic across runs and configs, so the same token id always maps to the same vector. With \(D = 32\) this gives a bounded, isotropic, zero-mean-in-expectation target in \(\{-1, +1\}^{32}\).

The model is CausalLMWithLinearHead (lines 57–105): a SmolLM2-135M backbone followed by a fresh nn.Linear(hidden_size, D, bias=False) head applied to the last-position hidden state. Head rows are randomly initialized and renormalized to unit norm via initial_output_norms = [1.0] * D. The whole stack is fine-tuned in bfloat16 inside torch.cuda.device(...) / torch.autocast(...) contexts.

title: Regression: corpus regression
text:
Optimization problem and evaluation metric

Population objective
Every method below estimates — through some surrogate — the same population MSE, \[
\mathcal{E}(\theta) \;:=\; \mathbb{E}_{x_{1:n} \sim p}\, \mathbb{E}_{x_{n+K} \sim p(\cdot \mid x_{1:n})}\, \bigl\lVert g_\theta(x_{1:n}) - f(x_{n+K}) \bigr\rVert^2.
\] The Bayes-optimal predictor is \(g^\ast(x_{1:n}) = \mathbb{E}\bigl[f(x_{n+K}) \mid x_{1:n}\bigr]\), achieving the intrinsic-variance lower bound \(\mathbb{E}\,\mathrm{Var}\bigl[f(x_{n+K}) \mid x_{1:n}\bigr]\). The NTP baseline (§4.1) is our proxy for this lower bound.


Held-out evaluation metric
Per-batch sufficient statistics \((xx_d, xy_d, yy_d, \sum_b f_\theta(x_b)_d, \sum_b y_{b,d}, n)\) are accumulated by RegressionStatCounter (src/metrics.py:56–62) and reduced to two scalars dim-averaged across \(D\) output coordinates (_scalar_corr_from_stats, state.py:121–131): \[
\widehat{\mathrm{mse}} \;=\; \frac{1}{D}\sum_{d=1}^{D} \frac{xx_d - 2\, xy_d + yy_d}{N},
\qquad
\widehat{\mathrm{corr}} \;=\; \frac{1}{D}\sum_{d=1}^{D} \frac{xy_d}{\sqrt{xx_d\, yy_d}}.
\]






Warning



corr is uncentered cosine similarity per dim, not Pearson. The dataset means \(\bar y_d\) are not subtracted in the numerator or denominator. For Rademacher labels \(\bar y_d \approx 0\) and the two coincide; for token_id labels (target mean far from zero) cosine \(\neq\) Pearson and the metric should be read accordingly. The same uncentered formula is applied at plot time in _decode_dim_averaged (analysis.py:90–114), so written numbers and plotted numbers always agree.




Train-window aggregate vs. held-out val
Each row of val_metrics.parquet carries two sets of sufficient stats: val_target_* is computed on the held-out validation set at every val step; train_target_* is the sum of the per-batch sufficient stats over all training batches between val flushes (TrainStepOutput in state.py:24–46; _serialize_val docstring at state.py:318–331). The latter is therefore a moving aggregate over changing model snapshots within the most recent val window — it is not a held-out train-set evaluation, so it tends to be noisier and slightly more pessimistic than a fresh-pass eval would give.

title: Regression: corpus regression
text:
Methods
The codebase implements six estimators, all targeting \(g_\theta \approx g^\ast\) but with different surrogate losses, gradient identities, and finite-\(R\) behaviours.

4.1 NTP baseline — inference-only proxy for \(g^\ast\)
src/experiments/corpus_regression/ntp_baseline.py:105–197.
Use the pretrained SmolLM2-135M next-token distribution \(p_\phi(\cdot \mid x_{1:n})\) directly: \[
\hat g(x_{1:n}) \;=\; \sum_{t \in V} p_\phi(t \mid x_{1:n})\, f(t) \;=\; \mathrm{softmax}\bigl(\mathrm{logits}\bigr)_{:,-1}\, \Phi,
\] where the label projector \(\Phi \in \mathbb{R}^{|V| \times D}\) is the Rademacher matrix or, for token-id labels, \(\Phi_{t} = (\mathrm{lo} + (\mathrm{hi}-\mathrm{lo})\cdot t / |V|)\) (lines 138–151). This is the exact closed form of \(\mathbb{E}_{t \sim p_\phi}[f(t)]\). Under the assumption \(p_\phi \approx p\), \(\hat g \approx g^\ast\) and the resulting val MSE upper-bounds the intrinsic variance — every other method’s MSE is benchmarked against it. No training is involved, so \(R\) does not apply.


4.2 SL — direct MSE regression
sl.py:25–70.
Surrogate is plain MSE on the deterministic last-position projection \(g_\theta(x) := f_\theta(x)\): \[
\mathcal{L}_{\text{SL}}(\theta) \;=\; \frac{1}{B D} \sum_{b,d} \bigl(g_\theta(x^{(b)})_d - y^{(b)}_d\bigr)^2.
\] The population gradient identity is the standard \(\nabla_\theta \mathcal{E}(\theta) = 2\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[(g_\theta(x) - y)\,\nabla_\theta g_\theta(x)\right]\), so the minibatch gradient is an unbiased Monte-Carlo estimate independent of any rollout count. SL is the reference all RL methods are compared against.


4.3 SL-CE — NTP cross-entropy with projected eval
sl_ce.py:312–398.
Trains the native SmolLM2 lm_head end-to-end (no swapped regression head). Training loss is plain cross-entropy on the lookahead token id: \[
\mathcal{L}_{\text{SL-CE}}(\theta) \;=\; -\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b} \log p_\theta\bigl(x^{(b)}_{n+K} \,\bigm|\, x^{(b)}_{1:n}\bigr).
\] Intermediate tokens are not exposed: the CE always fires at the \(K\)-th-ahead position. The current sweep uses \(K = 1\), but the formulation is well-defined for any \(K\).
For evaluation we project the softmax through the same label projector \(\Phi\) used by the NTP baseline, \[
\hat g_\theta(x_{1:n}) \;:=\; \mathrm{softmax}\bigl(\mathrm{logits}_\theta(x_{1:n})\bigr)_{:,-1}\, \Phi,
\] so val MSE / corr live in the same target space as SL/RL methods (sl_ce.py:336–351). As \(p_\theta \to p\) pointwise, \(\hat g_\theta \to g^\ast\). When \(f\) is bijective on \(V\) (e.g. token-id labels), CE on \(p_\theta\) is in fact a stronger training signal than SL on \(f\): \(p_\theta\) is a sufficient statistic for any downstream observation function.


4.4 RLOO — per-dim leave-one-out advantages
rloo.py:69–174.
Wrap the deterministic prediction in an isotropic Gaussian rollout policy \[
\pi_\theta(z \mid x) \;=\; \mathcal{N}\!\bigl(g_\theta(x),\, \sigma^2 I_D\bigr),
\] sample \(R\) rollouts \(z_1, \dots, z_R\) per prompt, and use the negative squared error as reward. With factorized=True (the canonical setting in vince-sweep.bash), the reward is per output dimension: \[
r_{j,d} \;=\; -(z_{j,d} - y_d)^2,
\qquad
A_{j,d} \;=\; r_{j,d} - \frac{1}{R-1}\sum_{i \neq j} r_{i,d} \;=\; \frac{R}{R-1}\bigl(r_{j,d} - \bar r_d\bigr).
\] (In factorized=False mode the reward is joint, \(r_j = -\lVert z_j - y\rVert^2\), and the same scalar \(A_j\) is broadcast across \(D\).) The per-dim log-policy drops \(\theta\)-independent constants: \[
\log \pi_\theta(z_j \mid x)_d \;=\; -\tfrac{1}{2\sigma^2}(z_{j,d} - g_\theta(x)_d)^2 + \mathrm{const}(\theta).
\] The surrogate loss in code (line 160) is \[
\mathcal{L}_{\text{RLOO}}(\theta) \;=\; -\frac{1}{B R}\sum_{b,j}\sum_d A_{j,d}\, \log \pi_\theta(z_j \mid x^{(b)})_d.
\]
Unbiasedness. REINFORCE gives \(\nabla_\theta \mathbb{E}_z[r(z)] = \mathbb{E}_z[r(z)\,\nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(z)]\). The leave-one-out baseline depends only on the peer rollouts \(z_{-j}\), so for the \(j\)-th term \[
\mathbb{E}\!\left[A_{j,d}\,\nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(z_j)_d \,\middle|\, z_{-j}\right]
\;=\; \mathbb{E}_{z_j}\!\left[r_{j,d}\,\nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(z_j)_d\right] - 0,
\] because the conditional baseline contribution kills under the score-function identity \(\mathbb{E}[\nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(z_j)] = 0\). Variance drops without bias.
Limit \(R \to \infty\). With Gaussian policy, \[
\mathbb{E}_{z \sim \mathcal{N}(g_\theta(x), \sigma^2 I)}\bigl[-\lVert z - y\rVert^2\bigr]
\;=\; -\lVert g_\theta(x) - y\rVert^2 - D\sigma^2,
\] so maximizing the population reward is identical to minimizing SL’s MSE up to a \(\theta\)-independent additive constant \(D\sigma^2\). RLOO’s expected gradient agrees with SL’s; only the Monte-Carlo variance (which the leave-one-out baseline reduces) separates them at finite \(R\).


4.5 GRPO — group-standardized advantages
grpo.py:21–139.
Same isotropic Gaussian policy as RLOO, joint reward \(r_j = -\lVert z_j - y\rVert^2\), but with group-standardized advantage \[
A_j \;=\; \frac{r_j - \bar r}{\mathrm{std}(r) + 10^{-8}}.
\] The surrogate loss couples the joint log-policy \(\log\pi_\theta(z_j \mid x) = -\tfrac{1}{2\sigma^2}\lVert z_j - g_\theta(x)\rVert^2 + \mathrm{const}\) to \(A_j\): \[
\mathcal{L}_{\text{GRPO}}(\theta) \;=\; -\frac{1}{B R}\sum_{b,j} A_j\, \log \pi_\theta(z_j \mid x^{(b)}).
\]
Unbiasedness — careful. Unlike the RLOO leave-one-out baseline, GRPO’s \(\mathrm{std}(r)\) divisor is computed from all \(z_{1:R}\), including \(z_j\). The score-function identity therefore does not cleanly collapse the baseline term, and GRPO targets a whitened surrogate of the REINFORCE gradient rather than the bare REINFORCE gradient. This is a deliberate variance-reduction / step-size-stabilization heuristic, not a bias-free reduction.
Limit \(R \to \infty\). \(\mathrm{std}(r) \to \sigma_r(\theta)\) deterministically, so the gradient direction approaches RLOO’s joint variant — which itself collapses to SL’s gradient direction by the calculation in §4.4 — modulo the multiplicative scalar \(1/\sigma_r(\theta)\).


4.6 MaxRL — leave-one-out U-statistic
maxrl.py:24–198; estimator in src/maxrl_estimator.py. Sketch + link; full DP derivation lives in MaxRL gradient estimator details.
Same Gaussian rollout policy. Define the per-rollout likelihood \(\ell(y, z) := \mathcal{N}(y;\, z,\, \sigma^2 I_D)\), supremum \(L = (2\pi\sigma^2)^{-D/2}\), and normalized \(\sigma_j := \ell(y, z_j) / L \in [0, 1]\). Let \(\sigma_\theta := \mathbb{E}_z[\sigma_j]\) be the marginal normalized likelihood.
Population objective. Degree-\(D\) Maclaurin truncation of \(\log \sigma_\theta\) about \(\sigma_\theta = 1\): \[
J_D(\theta) \;:=\; -\sum_{k=1}^{D} \frac{(1 - \sigma_\theta)^k}{k},
\qquad
J_\infty(\theta) \;=\; \log \sigma_\theta \;=\; \log \mathbb{E}_z\!\left[\ell(y, z)\right] - \log L.
\] This matches the \(\log \mathbb{E}_y \exp(-\lVert y - z\rVert^2)\) form in nogit_draft.tex up to additive constants.
Estimator. With subtract_baseline=True (canonical), \[
\hat g_D \;=\; \frac{1}{R}\sum_{j=1}^R \omega_j\, \sigma^{(\text{eff})}_j\, \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(z_j \mid x),
\qquad
\sigma^{(\text{eff})}_j \;=\; \frac{R}{R-1}\bigl(\sigma_j - \bar\sigma\bigr).
\] Each \(\omega_j\) is a leave-one-out U-statistic over the peer complements \(a_{-j} = (1 - \sigma_i)_{i \neq j}\), satisfying \(\mathbb{E}[\omega_j] = w_D(\sigma_\theta) := \sum_{d=0}^{D-1}(1 - \sigma_\theta)^d\). The U-statistic is computed in log-space via a bidiagonal-recurrence prefix/suffix scan; see gradient-estimator.qmd for the DP and numerics. Unbiasedness follows because \(\omega_j\) depends only on \(z_{-j}\) and the peer-mean baseline \(\bar\sigma_{-j} = (R\bar\sigma - \sigma_j)/(R-1)\) likewise decouples from \(z_j\).
Factorized vs joint. The canonical sweep uses use_factorized_likelihoods=True: each output dim is treated as an independent 1-D Gaussian regression with \(\ell_d(y_d, z_d) = \mathcal{N}(y_d; z_d, \sigma^2)\); the U-statistic runs per-dim. This caps \(\sigma_\theta \le 1/\sqrt 2\) regardless of \(D\), avoiding the \(2^{-D/2}\) collapse of the joint variant when \(D\) is large (maxrl.py:24–36, 99–127).
The surrogate loss in code (line 184) packages this as \[
\mathcal{L}_{\text{MaxRL}}(\theta) \;=\; -\frac{1}{B R}\sum_{b,j} \sum_d c_{b,j,d}\, \log \pi_\theta(z_j \mid x^{(b)})_d,
\qquad
c_{b,j,d} = \omega_{b,j,d}\, \sigma^{(\text{eff})}_{b,j,d}.
\]
Limit \(R \to \infty\) (with degree \(D = R\)). \(\hat g_D \to \nabla_\theta J_\infty(\theta) = \nabla_\theta \log \mathbb{E}_z[\ell(y, z)]\). For the Gaussian policy and Gaussian likelihood, the convolution identity gives \[
\mathbb{E}_{z \sim \mathcal{N}(g_\theta(x), \sigma^2 I)}\!\left[\mathcal{N}(y; z, \sigma^2 I)\right]
\;=\; \mathcal{N}\!\bigl(y;\, g_\theta(x),\, 2\sigma^2 I\bigr),
\] so \[
J_\infty(\theta) \;=\; -\frac{1}{4\sigma^2}\, \lVert g_\theta(x) - y\rVert^2 + \mathrm{const}.
\] MaxRL’s \(R \to \infty\) limit is therefore exactly SL’s MSE objective up to a positive scalar \(1/(4\sigma^2)\) and a \(\theta\)-independent additive constant.






Note



Limit-behaviour summary. As the per-prompt rollout count \(R\) (and MaxRL’s truncation degree \(D = R\)) goes to infinity, the GRPO / RLOO / MaxRL gradient estimators all converge to a positive multiple of the SL (MSE) gradient — RLOO via \(\mathbb{E}_z[-\lVert z - y\rVert^2] = -\lVert g_\theta(x) - y\rVert^2 - D\sigma^2\), MaxRL via the Gaussian-convolution identity above, and GRPO by reduction to RLOO’s joint variant. The three RL methods are best read as finite-\(R\) estimators of SL with different bias/variance trade-offs, not as fundamentally different objectives — a useful lens for the rollout sweeps below.

title: MaxRL gradient estimator details
text:
Reference implementation: src/maxrl_estimator.py.
We use the generalized MaxRL estimator in its leave-one-out form. Fix one batch row \((x, y)\), let \(L > 0\) be a known upper bound on the likelihood function \(l\), and draw \(R\) iid rollouts \(z_1, \dots, z_R \sim m_\theta(\cdot \mid x)\). Define detached per-rollout likelihoods, their normalizations, and score vectors \[
l_j := l(y, z_j) \in [0, L], \quad \sigma_j := l_j / L \in [0, 1], \quad S_j := \nabla_\theta \log m_\theta(z_j \mid x).
\] Further define the marginal normalized likelihood and the weight function \[
\sigma_\theta := \mathbb{E}[\sigma_j] \in (0, 1], \qquad w_D(\sigma_\theta) := \sum_{k=0}^{D-1} (1 - \sigma_\theta)^k.
\]

Population objective
The degree-\(D\) MaxRL objective is the degree-\(D\) Maclaurin truncation of \(\log \sigma_\theta\) about \(\sigma_\theta = 1\): \[
J_D(\theta) := -\sum_{k=1}^{D} \frac{(1 - \sigma_\theta)^k}{k}, \qquad \nabla_\theta J_D = w_D(\sigma_\theta) \, \mathbb{E}[\sigma_j \, S_j].
\] As \(D \to \infty\), \(J_D \to \log \sigma_\theta\) and the gradient recovers the exact log-likelihood gradient; at finite \(D\) the gradient residual is the geometric factor \(1 - (1 - \sigma_\theta)^D\).


Leave-one-out estimator
The generalized leave-one-out estimator has the form \[
\hat{g}_D(x, y) = \frac{1}{R} \sum_{j=1}^R \omega_j \, \sigma_j \, S_j,
\] where each \(\omega_j\) is built from the peer rollouts \(k \neq j\) only and satisfies \[
\mathbb{E}[\omega_j] = w_D(\sigma_\theta).
\]


Formulating the problem
Define the per-rollout complements \[
a_j := 1 - \sigma_j \in [0, 1] \implies w_D(\sigma_\theta) = \sum_{k=0}^{D-1} \mathbb{E}[a_j]^k.
\] For a list \((a_1, \dots, a_R) \in [0, 1]^R\), its \(k\)-th elementary symmetric polynomial is the sum of all size-\(k\) products: \[
e_k(a_1, \dots, a_R) := \sum_{1 \le i_1 < \cdots < i_k \le R} a_{i_1} \cdots a_{i_k}, \qquad e_0 := 1.
\]
Fix index \(j\). Its canonical leave-one-out peer set is \[
C_j := \{1, \dots, j-1, j+1, \dots, R\}.
\] We care about the normalized elementary symmetric polynomial for each element on its leave-one-out peer set, and, in particular, its sum; our gradient estimator depends on this weighting: \[
\omega_j = \sum_{k=0}^{D-1} \frac{e_k\bigl((a_i)_{i \in C_j}\bigr)}{\binom{R-1}{k}}
\] This yields a standalone programming problem.
Input. A batched tensor \(a \in [0, 1]^{B \times R}\) and an integer \(1 \le D \le R\).
Output. A batched tensor \(\omega \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times R}\) with entries \[
\omega_{b, j} = \sum_{k=0}^{D-1} \frac{e_k\bigl((a_{b, i})_{i \in C_j}\bigr)}{\binom{R-1}{k}}.
\]
Target complexity. An exact or mathematically equivalent formulation with:

\(O(BRD)\) time, \(O(BRD)\) memory.
no subtraction of nearly equal \(O(1)\) or larger terms.

The last requirement is the key numerical design constraint. A natural but unstable route is to compute full-sample coefficients and then “peel off” rollout \(j\) by subtraction. We empirically found that this leads to significant numerical errors for \(R \geq 32\), and digit-significance dependence grows approximately linearly in the number of rollouts.


State vectors and matrix view
Instead, we define states that are already normalized by the final peer count \(R - 1\). For any canonical subset \(I \subseteq \{1, \dots, R\}\), define the state vector \[
x(I) := \bigl(x_0(I), \dots, x_{D-1}(I)\bigr)^\top, \quad x_k(I) := \frac{e_k\bigl((a_i)_{i \in I}\bigr)}{\binom{R-1}{k}}.
\]
Two basic facts make this a good state space:

\(x_0(I) = 1\).
Because each \(a_i \in [0, 1]\), every forward-state coordinate is bounded \(0 \le x_k(I) \le 1\).

Now suppose \(I\) is a canonical subset and we append one new complement value \(a\). Using \[
e_k(I \cup \{a\}) = e_k(I) + a \, e_{k-1}(I),
\] we obtain the fixed-denominator recurrence over appending elements to the canonical set \[
x_0' = x_0, \quad x_k' = x_k + \frac{k}{R-k} \, a \, x_{k-1}, \qquad k = 1, \dots, D-1.
\] Package the update as multiplication by a lower-bidiagonal matrix \(M(a) \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times D}\): \[
x' = M(a) \, x \quad  \text{ where } \quad M(a)_{k, k} = 1,\quad  M(a)_{k, k-1} = \frac{k}{R-k} \, a
\]
With the empty-set initial state \[
e_0 := (1, 0, \dots, 0)^\top,
\] the state for any canonical prefix \(I = \{1, \dots, j\}\) is obtained by repeated application of these matrices.


Prefix-suffix scans
Define the forward prefix states so that \(\alpha_j = x(\{1, \dots, j\})\): \[
\alpha_0 := e_0, \qquad \alpha_j := M(a_j) \, \alpha_{j-1}, \qquad j = 1, \dots, R.
\] Similarly define the suffix covectors which encode the “suffix-and-sum” operation: \[
\beta_R^\top := \mathbf{1}^\top, \qquad \beta_{j-1}^\top := \beta_j^\top M(a_j), \qquad j = R, \dots, 1,
\]
Now fix rollout \(j\). The leave-one-out peer set \(C_j\) is the union of the canonical prefix before \(j\) and the canonical suffix after \(j\). Its state vector is therefore \[
x(C_j) = M(a_R) \cdots M(a_{j+1}) \, \alpha_{j-1} \implies \omega_j = \mathbf{1}^\top x(C_j) = \beta_j^\top \alpha_{j-1}.
\]


Algorithm
For one batch row, the algorithm is:

Convert normalized likelihoods to complements \(a_j = 1 - \sigma_j\).
Run a forward scan over \(j = 1, \dots, R\) using the lower-bidiagonal update \(M(a_j)\).
Run a backward scan over \(j = R, \dots, 1\) using the same update.
Form all leave-one-out weights via \(\omega_j = \beta_j^\top \alpha_{j-1}\).

Each matrix-vector or covector-matrix update touches only adjacent state coordinates, so each scan step costs \(O(D)\). The full batched computation therefore has the target complexity \(O(BRD)\).

title: Scalar-pretrain
text: The scalar-pretrain setup keeps the architecture of ordinary causal language model pretraining, including the native lm_head, but changes what supervision is allowed to see. The underlying corpus token at each position is treated as a hidden categorical state. The observed target is only a scalar label attached to that token, currently the token id normalized to \([0, 1]\).

title: Scalar-pretrain
text:
Problem setup
Fix a corpus distribution \(p\) over token sequences and a tokenizer vocabulary \(V\). In the canonical scalar-pretrain setting, each training row is a length \(T = 128\) token sequence \[
Z_{1:T} \sim p,
\] with a beginning-of-sequence token available as context for the first position. At autoregressive position \(i\), define \[
C_i := (Z_0, Z_1, \dots, Z_{i-1}), \qquad Z_0 := \mathrm{BOS},
\] so the model predicts the hidden current token \(Z_i\) from its teacher-forced prefix \(C_i\). This gives \(T\) supervised positions per row, not only the final position.
The observed scalar label is a deterministic map \[
\varphi : V \to [0, 1].
\] For the current token-id label, \[
Y_i := \varphi(Z_i), \qquad
\varphi(t) := \frac{t}{|V|}
\]
Every method uses the same causal transformer and the same native LM head. Let the logits at position \(i\) be \[
a_{\theta, i}(t) \in \mathbb{R}, \qquad t \in V,
\] and let the LM-head induced categorical distribution be \[
q_{\theta, i}(t \mid C_i)
  := \frac{\exp a_{\theta, i}(t)}
          {\sum_{u \in V} \exp a_{\theta, i}(u)}.
\] The scalar prediction used for evaluation is the softmax-projected mean \[
\mu_{\theta, i}(C_i)
  := \mathbb{E}_{t \sim q_{\theta, i}(\cdot \mid C_i)}[\varphi(t)]
  = \sum_{t \in V} q_{\theta, i}(t \mid C_i)\,\varphi(t).
\]
